summary: Guidance on how the IETF should consider new congestion control algorithms that differ from standard ones, since using them on the global Internet could affect other traffic. It urges caution. It is a best current practice and was replaced by RFC 9743.

eli5.summary: Rules for carefully checking new ways of sharing the internet before everybody uses them. A newer RFC replaced this.

questions: how to specify new congestion control algorithms
what makes a congestion control algorithm safe
how should i test a new congestion control scheme
subtitle: Guidelines for designing and evaluating new congestion control algorithms.

tldr.problem: New congestion control algorithms designed for high-speed networks and special environments could harm standard TCP traffic or cause other Internet problems if deployed globally without careful evaluation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides eight detailed guidelines for authors and the IETF community to evaluate new algorithms, covering impact on standard protocols, performance in difficult environments, protection against congestion collapse, fairness, and deployment considerations.
tldr.outcome: New congestion control schemes are now published as Experimental RFCs with clear statements about safety and deployment scope. The procedure was updated by RFC 9743.

facts.label: Experimental classes
facts.value: 2 (safe for internet deployment; safe for research only)

today: RFC 5033 is a Best Current Practice. It was superseded by RFC 9743, which updates the guidelines for congestion control in light of subsequent research, new transport mechanisms like QUIC, and experience with deployments.

sections.title: Why New Congestion Control Needs Careful Evaluation
sections.content:
Congestion control is how computers on the internet share bandwidth when the network gets busy. Standard TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) has used the same basic congestion control for decades, but it performs poorly in some modern environments, like high-speed networks or satellite links. Researchers have proposed many alternative algorithms that work better in these cases.

However, deploying a new congestion control algorithm globally creates risk. If an algorithm is too aggressive, it could starve standard TCP flows of bandwidth. If it fails to back off when the network is congested, it could contribute to congestion collapse. RFC 5033 provides guidance for the IETF to evaluate new proposals carefully before allowing them onto the public Internet.
sections.eli5: A new way of sharing bandwidth might work great in one situation but break things in another. The IETF needs to test new algorithms carefully before everyone uses them.

sections.title: Classification of Experimental Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RFC defines two classes of Experimental congestion control algorithms. Class 1 algorithms are judged safe enough to deploy for best-effort traffic on the global Internet, though they are still being studied. Examples like HighSpeed TCP (RFC 3649) fit here. Class 2 algorithms are promising but not yet deemed safe for widespread deployment. They may be specified to enable research in simulation, testbeds, or controlled environments like private networks. The Quick-Start mechanism (RFC 4782) is a Class 2 example.

All Experimental congestion control RFCs must include a statement in their abstract indicating which class they belong to and explicitly listing the environments where the algorithm is not safe or not recommended. An algorithm might be safe (will not break) but still not recommended (will not perform well) in certain conditions.
sections.eli5: Some new algorithms are safe to test on the real internet; others are only safe to test in labs. Every RFC has to say which kind it is.

sections.title: Eight Guidelines for Evaluating New Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC outlines eight key criteria. (1) Differences from standard principles: authors must explain how they diverge from RFC 2914's congestion control principles. (2) Impact on standard protocols: the new algorithm should be evaluated competing against TCP, SCTP, and DCCP to understand any unfairness. (3) Difficult environments: authors should test in wireless networks, high-latency paths, and other challenging conditions. (4) Range of environments: evaluation across different bandwidths, round-trip times, and queueing behaviors reveals where the algorithm breaks down.

(5) Congestion collapse protection: the algorithm must either back off significantly when packet loss is high, or must perform full backoff—eventually reducing to one packet per round-trip time and exponentially backing off further if congestion persists. (6) Fairness: when multiple flows use the same algorithm, bandwidth should be shared equitably. (7) Misbehavior and attacks: the algorithm should be analyzed for robustness against misbehaving nodes and malicious actors. (8) Incremental deployment: authors should discuss whether the algorithm can be deployed gradually and what happens when it meets legacy equipment.
sections.eli5: Test it in different networks, check it does not starve other traffic, check it does not break under extreme congestion, test with bad actors, test when it meets old equipment.

sections.title: Minimum Requirements for Global Deployment
sections.content:
For an Experimental algorithm to be approved for widespread deployment on the global Internet, it must meet stricter minimum requirements. The proposal must satisfy guidelines (1), (3), (4), (5), and (8): it must explain deviations from standard principles, work in difficult environments, be tested across a range of scenarios, include congestion collapse protection, and support incremental deployment.

For guidelines (2), (6), and (7)—impact on standard traffic, fairness, and robustness—the author must perform the evaluation and provide analysis. If the proposed mechanism has significantly more problems than TCP, it should not be approved for global Internet deployment. This minimum threshold does not require TCP-friendliness in all environments, but it does require that the proposal not cause widespread harm.
sections.eli5: For a new algorithm to use everywhere on the internet, it has to pass stricter checks: work on difficult networks, protect the network during extreme congestion, and not break too many other things.

sections.title: Publishing and Scope of New Algorithms
sections.content:
New congestion control algorithms should be published as Experimental RFCs with a clear statement of their intended scope and safety. Authors not yet ready to standardize can publish internet-drafts or submit Informational RFCs as a first step, though these should include explicit warnings against use on the global Internet.

For algorithms intended only for specific environments, the proposal should address how the scope restriction is enforced. Some algorithms may rely on documentation alone, while others may require protocol mechanisms to prevent inappropriate deployment. The RFC notes that the IETF's processes for publication outside the standards track (such as IRTF and Independent Submissions via the RFC Editor) are not changing, though the IESG may add notes to such documents based on these guidelines.
sections.eli5: If an algorithm is only safe in labs, that has to be stated clearly in the RFC. The author also has to think about how to stop people from using it in the wrong place.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 5033 is a Best Current Practice. It was superseded by RFC 9743, which updated the guidelines for specifying new congestion control algorithms in light of subsequent experience and new transport mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A newer RFC, 9743, replaced this with updated rules based on lessons learned.

items.title: Explain deviations
items.text: Show how the proposal differs from standard principles.

items.title: Evaluate impact on TCP
items.text: Test performance when competing with standard TCP, SCTP, DCCP.

items.title: Test difficult environments
items.text: Wireless, high latency, high packet loss, satellite.

items.title: Test varied conditions
items.text: Different bandwidths, RTTs, and levels of statistical multiplexing.

items.title: Prevent collapse
items.text: Back off aggressively or perform full exponential backoff under extreme congestion.

items.title: Ensure fairness
items.text: Bandwidth should be shared equitably among competing flows.

items.title: Consider misbehavior
items.text: Analyze robustness against misbehaving or malicious nodes.

items.title: Plan deployment
items.text: Show how the algorithm can be deployed gradually with legacy equipment.
